docsClusterPrereqs.title: Cluster prerequisites
docsClusterPrereqs.intro: Everything a Kubernetes cluster needs to have installed before you register it with Astrolift. Most clusters provisioned by astrolift-opscode already include these; this guide is for operators bringing their own cluster.
docsClusterPrereqs.cliBody: For a one-shot install of the prereqs below, driver-tuned for your provider, run <cmd>{command}</cmd> from your terminal. The CLI plants Flux + the platform's umbrella chart, then the cluster detail page's bootstrap card lets you reconcile the selection over time. <link>Install the CLI</link>.
docsClusterPrereqs.whenBody: Astrolift treats a tenant cluster as a runtime that hosts apps; it does not install or own infrastructure components in the cluster itself. Custom-domain TLS, ingress routing, and autoscaling are delegated to controllers that need to exist before Astrolift can use them. The checks below confirm the cluster is wired correctly; if any are missing, the matching features stay disabled and the control plane surfaces a remediation hint on the cluster detail page.
docsClusterPrereqs.requiredBody: Without these, registration succeeds but app workloads cannot accept inbound traffic on a custom hostname.
docsClusterPrereqs.certManagerBody: Issues and renews TLS certificates for custom domains. Astrolift creates Certificate resources on your behalf; cert-manager handles the ACME dance with Let's Encrypt (or whichever ClusterIssuer you configure). Without cert-manager the custom-domains workflow refuses to bind hostnames.
docsClusterPrereqs.ingressBody: Astrolift renders one ingress resource per app whose spec.ingressClassName matches an IngressClass that exists in the cluster. Any of the following controllers is fine; pick the one your platform team already runs.
docsClusterPrereqs.istioNote: When Astrolift detects Istio it emits Gateway + VirtualService resources instead of Ingress.
docsClusterPrereqs.albBody: On EKS, the ALB controller exposes services through an alb IngressClass. On GKE, the Gateway API controller ships with the cluster; install gateway-api CRDs to use it.
docsClusterPrereqs.externalDnsBody: Reads the hostnames from Certificate.spec.dnsNames / ingress resources and creates the corresponding records at your DNS provider. Required when you want Astrolift to fully self-serve custom-domain publication; otherwise an operator has to add CNAMEs by hand.
docsClusterPrereqs.externalDnsProviders: Supported providers with controller-friendly APIs include AWS Route53, Google Cloud DNS, Azure DNS, and Cloudflare. See <link>the upstream provider list</link> for the full set.
docsClusterPrereqs.recommendedBody: Astrolift works without these, but specific features stay off until they are present.
docsClusterPrereqs.storageBody: Required for in-cluster managed services that claim PersistentVolumeClaims, for example the in-cluster Postgres operator, in-cluster Redis, or any app that mounts a PVC directly. If every app you run uses an external RDS/Cloud SQL managed service, you can skip this.
docsClusterPrereqs.metricsBody: The Kubernetes HorizontalPodAutoscaler reads CPU / memory from metrics.k8s.io; without metrics-server autoscaling rules sit idle at the current replica count. Astrolift falls back to manual replica counts but the autoscale tab on app detail surfaces a banner explaining what's missing.
docsClusterPrereqs.prometheusBody: When Astrolift detects a reachable Prometheus it points the app metrics panels at it. Without one the panels render synthetic time-series so the UI stays useful in dev, but real workload numbers require Prometheus or another Prometheus-compatible scraper.
docsClusterPrereqs.verifyBody: Run these from a workstation that can reach the cluster. If any check fails, the matching feature stays disabled in Astrolift.
docsClusterPrereqs.troubleCertBody: Almost always an ACME challenge problem. For dns-01: the issuer has no credentials to write the TXT record (check the ClusterIssuer spec, then the controller pod logs for credential errors). For http-01: the validator pod cannot reach {url}; make sure the ingress controller is exposed publicly. Inspect with:
docsClusterPrereqs.troubleIngressBody: The Service the ingress points at has zero ready endpoints. Most often: the app pods are still pulling the image, the readiness probe is failing, or the Service selector doesn't match the pod labels. Confirm with {command}; if the address list is empty the ingress has nothing to forward to.
docsClusterPrereqs.troubleDnsBody: Two common causes: (a) RBAC: the controller's service account needs list/watch on services, ingresses, and the provider's CRDs, plus IAM/credentials to call the DNS provider's API; (b) ownership: external-dns refuses to modify a record it didn't create unless the TXT owner-id marker matches. Check the controller logs for skipping endpoint messages.
docsClusterPrereqs.troubleHpaTitle: HPA shows {unknown} for the target metric.
docsClusterPrereqs.troubleHpaBody: metrics-server is not installed or not scraping. Run kubectl top pods; if it errors with Metrics API not available, metrics-server is the fix.
docsClusterPrereqs.relatedCustomDomains: <link>Custom domains</link>: the feature that depends on cert-manager and an ingress controller being present.
docsClusterPrereqs.relatedGetStarted: <link>Get started</link>: bring up the Astrolift stack locally before pointing it at a tenant cluster.

docsSourceProviders.title: Source providers
docsSourceProviders.intro: Connect Astrolift to GitHub or GitLab so a git push triggers a deploy.
docsSourceProviders.whenBody: You want to register an app whose source lives on a hosted Git provider, and have Astrolift watch a branch (or pull requests) so merges and pushes turn into deploys automatically. Without a connected source provider, apps are still deployable from manifests and registry images, but the push-to-deploy loop is unavailable.
docsSourceProviders.prereqPermission: Permission. An operator role that includes scm.connect (Owner and Admin have it by default).
docsSourceProviders.prereqAdmin: Admin access to the GitHub org or GitLab group. The Astrolift App is installed at the org / group level, not on individual users, so an org owner has to approve it.
docsSourceProviders.prereqUrl: Your install's public URL. GitHub and GitLab need to reach Astrolift to deliver webhooks. The backend reads this from APP_BASE_URL; verify it points at the public hostname users hit, not a private IP.
docsSourceProviders.githubIntro: The fastest path. Astrolift submits a GitHub App manifest on your behalf; you only have to approve the permissions and pick which repos the App can see.
docsSourceProviders.openProvidersGitHub: Go to Settings · Source providers and click Connect to GitHub.
docsSourceProviders.githubOrgBody: Type the org slug (the part of the URL after github.com/) and click Continue on GitHub. Astrolift submits a one-shot manifest containing the App name, callback URLs, webhook URL, and the permissions it requests.
docsSourceProviders.githubApproveBody: GitHub shows the permissions the Astrolift App requires:
docsSourceProviders.permContents: contents: read: clone source at deploy time
docsSourceProviders.permChecks: checks: write: report build / deploy status on commits
docsSourceProviders.githubCreate: Click {button}. GitHub creates the App, installs it on the org, and redirects you back to Astrolift.
docsSourceProviders.githubReposBody: The connection now appears under Hosts. When you register a new app from Apps · Register app, its onboarding wizard browses the repos the App was granted access to. To widen or narrow that set, edit the install on GitHub ({url}).
docsSourceProviders.gitlabIntro: GitLab does not have a manifest API equivalent to GitHub Apps, so this flow is a few extra clicks: register an OAuth application on GitLab, then paste the credentials back into Astrolift.
docsSourceProviders.openProvidersGitLab: Go to Settings · Source providers and click Connect to GitLab.
docsSourceProviders.gitlabGroupBody: Type your GitLab group slug. The instance URL defaults to https://gitlab.com; change it if you run a self-managed instance.
docsSourceProviders.gitlabRegisterTitle: Register an Astrolift application on GitLab
docsSourceProviders.gitlabRegisterBody: Click Open GitLab Applications. In the new tab, create a Group-owned application with these settings:
docsSourceProviders.gitlabSaveBody: Save. GitLab shows the Application ID and Secret exactly once.
docsSourceProviders.gitlabPasteBody: Return to Astrolift, paste the Application ID and Secret into the dialog, and save. The connection appears under Hosts and you can register apps from any project in the group.
docsSourceProviders.troubleHookBody: GitHub or GitLab can't reach the callback. This is operator-side: set APP_BASE_URL in the backend environment to the public URL of your install (the same hostname users hit), then re-run the connect flow.

docsPolicies.title: ABAC policies
docsPolicies.intro: Fine-grained access rules that layer on top of role bindings. Policies never grant beyond a role; they only carve out additional allow or deny conditions.
docsPolicies.whenBody: Astrolift's built-in roles cover most teams. Reach for policies when you need something the role catalog can't express. For example:
docsPolicies.exampleSenior: Only senior engineers can deploy to apps named prod-*.
docsPolicies.exampleNight: Nobody can write secrets between 22:00 and 06:00 UTC unless they're paged.
docsPolicies.exampleMfa: Pre-production deploys require an MFA factor that's less than 60 minutes old.
docsPolicies.exampleContractors: Contractors can read everything in a project but cannot change resource quotas.
docsPolicies.prereqModel: Mental model of ABAC vs RBAC. RBAC asks “does this user's role include this permission?” ABAC asks “given the attributes of this request (who, what, when, where), does any policy say deny?” A request only succeeds if RBAC allows it and no policy denies it.
docsPolicies.createBody: Open Settings · Policies and click New policy. Each policy has the following fields:
docsPolicies.fieldScopeBody: The breadth of the policy. ORG policies evaluate on every request; APP policies only evaluate when the request targets that specific app. Narrower scope = less evaluation cost and easier to reason about.
docsPolicies.fieldEffectBody: What happens when the policy matches. DENY always wins: if any policy at any scope denies, the request fails, even if a narrower-scope ALLOW also matches.
docsPolicies.fieldActionBody: Glob over permission slugs. app.deploy matches one exact slug; app.* matches every action on the app resource; * matches everything.
docsPolicies.fieldResourceBody: Glob over resource identifiers. app:prod-* matches apps whose slug starts with prod-; project:billing/* matches everything in the billing project.
docsPolicies.fieldActorBody: Who the policy applies to. Match by user ID, role slug, or both. Empty {empty} matches every actor.
docsPolicies.fieldConditionsBody: Extra predicates evaluated at request time. Available keys: time_of_day, day_of_week, ip_cidr, mfa_max_age_seconds, env.
docsPolicies.exampleSeniorBody: Only members of the senior-eng role can deploy any app whose slug starts with prod-.
docsPolicies.exampleSeniorOutcome: A senior engineer's deploy passes the role check (role_slug_not_in returns false → policy does not match → no deny). Anyone else trips the deny and the deploy fails with a permission error.
docsPolicies.exampleFreezeBody: Nobody can write secrets between 22:00 and 06:00 UTC; used during incident windows or change-freeze periods.
docsPolicies.troubleEffectBody: DENY always wins. Check for a broader-scope DENY (ORG-level) that already covers the request. The policies table shows the matching order; sort by scope.
docsPolicies.troubleButtonTitle: A user sees a button they shouldn't.
docsPolicies.troubleButtonBody: The UI hides controls based on RBAC, not ABAC; the button stays visible because the role technically grants the action, but the request fails at the resolver when ABAC denies. Either tighten the role binding, or surface the ABAC outcome in the UI via <link>Permissions diagnostic</link>.
docsPolicies.troubleJsonBody: The dialog validates on save and returns a precise error (“unknown key time_of_the_day, did you mean time_of_day?”). Re-open the policy to see the stored value.
docsPolicies.relatedIdentityProviders: <link>Identity providers</link>: who can sign in. Policies decide what they can do once they have.
docsPolicies.relatedDiagnostic: <link>Permissions diagnostic</link>: debug a specific user's effective permissions on a specific resource.

docsCustomDomains.title: Custom domains
docsCustomDomains.intro: Bring your own hostname (for example app.acme.com) and let Astrolift handle TLS via cert-manager.
docsCustomDomains.prereqNote: Cluster prerequisites. This guide assumes the tenant cluster already runs cert-manager and an ingress controller. If you're bringing your own cluster, work through Cluster prerequisites first.
docsCustomDomains.whenBody: Every app gets a generated *.astrolift.app subdomain by default. You only need this guide when you want a branded hostname like app.acme.com or checkout.acme.com in front of your workload, with automatic TLS managed by cert-manager inside the tenant cluster.
docsCustomDomains.prereqCluster: A connected cluster. The app is deployed to a tenant cluster that has cert-manager and the ingress controller installed (this is the default for clusters provisioned by opscode).
docsCustomDomains.prereqDns: DNS you can edit. You need access to the DNS provider that holds the parent zone so you can add a CNAME (or TXT) record.
docsCustomDomains.prereqPermission: Permission. An operator role that includes app.update; Owner, Admin, and Deployer have this by default.
docsCustomDomains.step1Body: Navigate to your app, then click the Domains tab. You will see any hostnames already bound to the app and a button to add a new one.
docsCustomDomains.step2Title: Enter the FQDN and validation method
docsCustomDomains.step2Body: Type the full hostname. The validation method defaults to <badge>dns-01</badge> which works for both apex and wildcard records and does not require the hostname to be publicly reachable before issuance. Leave it blank to accept the platform default.
docsCustomDomains.step3Title: Astrolift returns the record to publish
docsCustomDomains.step3Body: After you save, the row appears with a pending_validation cert state and a validation token. For dns-01 this is a TXT record at _acme-challenge.app.acme.com; for http-01 it is a CNAME pointing at the cluster ingress. Click the token to copy it.
docsCustomDomains.step4Title: Publish the record at your DNS provider
docsCustomDomains.step4Body: Add the record verbatim. Most providers propagate within a minute or two, but TTLs are advisory; give it up to ~10 minutes before you escalate to troubleshooting.
docsCustomDomains.step5Body: Astrolift polls every ~30 seconds. Once the record is visible from its resolvers, cert-manager issues the certificate and the row transitions pending_validation → validated → active. You can force an immediate poll with the Recheck button on the row.
docsCustomDomains.authBody: If your cluster has an edge login gate, it covers the app's platform subdomain, not your custom domain. The gate's session cookie is issued by the cluster's auth host and scoped to the platform's own zone, and a response from one domain cannot set a cookie for an unrelated one. A custom domain is therefore outside the gate by construction, and no setting changes that.
docsCustomDomains.authMarker: The Domains tab marks any such row {label}, and the Ingress carries astrolift.dev/edge-auth=ungated so it is visible from kubectl too. Treat a custom domain as a public entrance: if the app behind it needs authentication, it has to enforce that itself.
docsCustomDomains.troublePendingBody: DNS likely has not propagated to the issuing resolvers. Check from an outside network:
docsCustomDomains.troubleValidationBody: The TXT record value must match the token verbatim: no surrounding quotes, no trailing whitespace, no smart-quoted characters (copy/paste from a terminal, not from a doc).
docsCustomDomains.troubleCaaBody: If the parent zone has a CAA record that does not list letsencrypt.org, ACME cannot issue. Add a CAA entry allowing Let's Encrypt, or remove the restrictive record.
docsCustomDomains.troubleExpiredTitle: Cert expired and was not rotated.
docsCustomDomains.troubleExpiredBody: cert-manager auto-renews ~30 days before expiry. If it has not, an operator can inspect the cert-manager logs in the tenant cluster; the rotation Workflow re-heals on the next periodic tick.

docsIdentityProviders.title: Identity providers
docsIdentityProviders.intro: Route sign-in through your corporate IdP: OIDC, SAML, Cognito, Auth0, Okta, Azure AD, Google Workspace, GitHub, or local accounts.
docsIdentityProviders.whenBody: You want users to sign in with their existing corporate identity instead of a separate Astrolift password, and you want central control over who has access (deprovision in the IdP, lose access here). Exactly one provider is active at a time; the rest are standby.
docsIdentityProviders.prereqPermission: Permission. An operator role with org.update (Owner and Admin have it).
docsIdentityProviders.prereqAdmin: Admin access to the IdP. You will register a new OIDC or SAML client there.
docsIdentityProviders.prereqRedirect: Astrolift's redirect URI. Visible in the New provider dialog. Format is {uri}. Every IdP needs this exact value in its allowed callback list.
docsIdentityProviders.configureBody: Pick the matching subsection. Every kind ends with the same three clicks in Astrolift: Settings · Identity providers → New provider → pick the kind → paste the credentials → Make active.
docsIdentityProviders.allowlistBody: By default, an SSO sign-in succeeds only if Astrolift already has an account for that user. To let new users self-onboard, mark their email domains as trusted.
docsIdentityProviders.allowlistStep2: Scroll to the Trusted email domains card and add corp.com (no @).
docsIdentityProviders.allowlistStep3: Save. Anyone who signs in via SSO with an @corp.com email is auto-joined to the organization with the default member role.
docsIdentityProviders.troubleNoIdpBody: The install's bootstrap_idp environment variables were not set. Configure a provider from Settings · Identity providers and set it active.
docsIdentityProviders.troubleRedirectTitle: Login redirects to the wrong host (or returns redirect_uri_mismatch).
docsIdentityProviders.troubleRedirectBody: APP_BASE_URL in the backend and the redirect URI registered at the IdP must match exactly: protocol, host, path, and trailing slash.
docsIdentityProviders.troubleSignupBody: The user's email domain isn't in the trusted list. See <link>Domain allowlist</link> above.
docsIdentityProviders.troubleSamlBody: The IdP rotated its signing certificate. Re-paste the metadata URL (or upload the fresh XML); Astrolift refreshes the trust store on save.

oidc.title: Generic OIDC
oidc.intro: The most flexible option. Works with any provider that publishes an OpenID Connect discovery document.

steps.s1: At the IdP, register a new OIDC client. Paste the redirect URI shown in the Astrolift dialog (it ends with /app/auth1/callback).
steps.s2: Copy the client_id, client_secret, and the discovery URL (the .well-known/openid-configuration endpoint).
steps.s3: In Astrolift, open Settings · Identity providers · New provider, pick OIDC, paste the values, and Make active.

cognito.title: Amazon Cognito
cognito.intro: Cognito user pools speak OIDC. Use this when your install lives in AWS and you already manage users in a pool.

steps.s1: In the AWS console, open the user pool · App integration · Create an app client. Pick a confidential client and add the Astrolift redirect URI.
steps.s2: Note the User Pool ID, App client ID, and App client secret. The discovery URL is {url}.
steps.s3: In Astrolift, New provider · Cognito, paste the three values, Make active.

auth0.title: Auth0
auth0.intro: Auth0 is the default for Calliope AI-hosted installs. Use Auth0 if you want hosted MFA, passwordless, or social logins without running them yourself.

steps.s1: In Auth0, Applications · Create Application · Regular Web App. Set Allowed Callback URLs to the redirect URI from the Astrolift dialog.
steps.s2: Copy the Domain, Client ID, and Client Secret. The discovery URL is {url}.
steps.s3: In Astrolift, New provider · Auth0, paste the values, Make active.

okta.title: Okta
okta.intro: Okta is the most common enterprise choice. Use Okta's OIDC, not the SAML app; OIDC integrates cleanly with Astrolift's session model.

steps.s1: In Okta admin, Applications · Create App Integration · OIDC · Web Application. Add the Astrolift redirect URI under Sign-in redirect URIs.
steps.s2: Copy the Client ID, Client Secret, and the Issuer URL (visible under General · OpenID Connect ID Token).
steps.s3: In Astrolift, New provider · Okta, paste the values, Make active.

azureAd.title: Azure AD / Entra ID
azureAd.intro: Entra (formerly Azure AD) is the right pick if your org is on Microsoft 365.

steps.s1: In the Azure portal, App registrations · New registration. Set the redirect URI to the value from Astrolift and platform to Web.
steps.s2: Under Certificates & secrets, create a client secret and copy its value. Note the Application (client) ID and Directory (tenant) ID.
steps.s3: The discovery URL is {url}. Paste it plus the client ID and secret into Astrolift, Make active.

google.title: Google Workspace
google.intro: Google Workspace OIDC works when every Astrolift operator has a workspace account.

steps.s1: In Google Cloud console, APIs & Services · Credentials · Create OAuth client ID · Web application. Add the Astrolift redirect URI.
steps.s2: Copy the Client ID and Client Secret. The discovery URL is {url}.
steps.s3: In Astrolift, New provider · Google, paste the values, Make active. Combine with the domain allowlist below to limit sign-in to your workspace.

github.title: GitHub OAuth
github.intro: GitHub for sign-in only (independent of the SCM connection from Source providers). Useful for small teams that already have a GitHub org.

steps.s1: In GitHub, Settings · Developer settings · OAuth Apps · New OAuth App. Set the callback URL to the value from Astrolift.
steps.s2: Copy the Client ID and generate a Client Secret.
steps.s3: In Astrolift, New provider · GitHub OAuth, paste the values, Make active.

saml.title: SAML 2.0
saml.intro: For IdPs that only speak SAML (older enterprise installs, some federated setups).

steps.s1: At the IdP, register a new SAML application. Set the ACS URL and Entity ID to the values shown in the Astrolift dialog.
steps.s2: Download the IdP metadata XML or copy its URL.
steps.s3: In Astrolift, New provider · SAML, paste the metadata URL (or upload the XML), Make active.

local.title: Local accounts
local.intro: First-run / fallback only. Local accounts let an operator log in with a username and password stored in the Astrolift database. Use them while you are wiring an SSO provider, then turn them off.

steps.s1: Local accounts are enabled by default on a fresh install. The bootstrap admin lives in the database; see the install runbook for how it is seeded.
steps.s2: Once SSO is configured and verified, set the SSO provider active and either delete the local entry or block password sign-in via policy.

docsConfiguration.title: Configuration
docsConfiguration.intro: Every environment variable Astrolift reads at runtime. Source = <outline>{operator}</outline> means the operator sets it, <outline>{image}</outline> means the container image bakes a default in, and <secondary>{platform}</secondary> means Astrolift writes it into the workload at deploy time.
docsConfiguration.conventionRequired: Vars marked required either have no default or have a default that's only safe for local development (e.g. not-a-secret).
docsConfiguration.conventionUnlisted: Anything not listed here is not read by Astrolift; it is silently ignored if set.
docsConfiguration.mineNote: The reference is the same for everyone, so Mine is empty.
docsConfiguration.inspectBody: The Django management command features prints the current feature-flag state, and python manage.py diffsettings shows every Django setting against its default. The control plane never echoes secret values; settings marked sensitive print as ***.
docsConfiguration.relatedGetStarted: <link>Get started</link>: bring the stack up locally; env vars there default to the docker-compose service names.

docsWebhookEvents.title: Webhook events
docsWebhookEvents.intro: Every event type Astrolift emits via outbound webhooks, with the payload schema and a realistic JSON example for each. For setup and signature verification, see the <link>webhooks guide</link>.
docsWebhookEvents.envelopeBody: Every delivery shares the same outer envelope. The event-specific fields live under payload. Optional envelope fields may be empty strings; client receivers should treat missing / empty as the absence of a value.
docsWebhookEvents.eventIdNote: event_id is a ULID: globally unique, time-sortable. Use it for idempotency keys on your side.
docsWebhookEvents.deliveryIdNote: delivery_id is unique per attempt; retries reuse the same event_id with a new delivery_id.
docsWebhookEvents.schemaVersionNote: schema_version follows semver; payload-breaking changes bump the major.
docsWebhookEvents.signatureBody: Every delivery is signed with an X-Astrolift-Signature header (HMAC-SHA256 of {signed}, hex-encoded, prefixed with sha256=). The webhooks guide covers verification in Python, Node, and Go: read the raw body before any JSON parsing, and use a constant-time compare.
docsWebhookEvents.subscribingBody: To subscribe a receiver to one or more of these events, see the Create a subscription steps. The event-type field accepts either the exact slug (e.g. deployment.failed) or a wildcard:
docsWebhookEvents.wildcardCategory: deployment.*: every event in the deployments category.
docsWebhookEvents.relatedWebhooks: <link>Webhooks</link>: create a subscription, verify signatures, troubleshoot deliveries.
docsWebhookEvents.relatedPolicies: <link>ABAC policies</link>: restrict who can create webhook subscriptions in your organization.

docsIntroduction.title: Introduction
docsIntroduction.tagline: Build, deploy and operate with Astrolift.
docsIntroduction.whatBody: Astrolift is a control plane for applications and agents running on Kubernetes. Connect your clusters and source repositories, register an Astrolift manifest, and manage deployments, environment configuration and managed services from one dashboard or the CLI.
docsIntroduction.whatBody2: The control plane records desired configuration and deployment history. Cluster agents report observed runtime state; unavailable observations remain distinct from healthy or failed workloads.
docsIntroduction.conceptOrgs: Organizations, teams and projects organize ownership and access to apps, clusters and shared resources.
docsIntroduction.conceptApps: Applications and manifests describe workloads, configuration and service bindings. A registered app connects that definition to its source repository.
docsIntroduction.conceptEnvironments: Environments select runtime placement and environment-specific configuration for an app.
docsIntroduction.conceptDeployments: Deployments track image versions, approval requirements, execution and history for an environment.
docsIntroduction.conceptRoles: Roles, policies and credentials control permitted operations and resource scope. A token cannot expand its holder's access.
docsIntroduction.runtimeBody: The dashboard and CLI call the Django and Strawberry GraphQL control plane. PostgreSQL stores platform records, Redis supports caching, and Temporal coordinates long-running lifecycle work. Applications run on connected Kubernetes clusters rather than inside the dashboard process.
docsIntroduction.startQuickstart: <link>Quickstart</link> walks through connecting a cluster and source, registering an app and deploying it.
docsIntroduction.startPrerequisites: <link>Cluster prerequisites</link> describes the runtime services your cluster needs.
docsIntroduction.startLocalDev: <link>Local development setup</link> explains how contributors run the control plane locally.

docsGetStarted.title: Local development setup
docsGetStarted.intro: Run the Astrolift control plane from an astrolift-app checkout.
docsGetStarted.note: For your first application deployment, follow the <quickstart>Quickstart</quickstart>. The steps here are for contributors running the local control plane. They require Docker Desktop or Docker Engine with Compose v2. Review the <configuration>configuration reference</configuration> and your local environment files before starting the stack.
docsGetStarted.prepareBody: Run these commands from the repository root. Bootstrap checks Docker and creates missing local environment files from the examples. Fill in required configuration values before starting the Compose services. The stack includes the API and UI, PostgreSQL, Redis, Temporal, and local storage and email services.
docsGetStarted.migrateTitle: Migrate and seed the local identity
docsGetStarted.migrateBody: Once the API container is running, apply the database migrations and run the development identity seed. This creates the local organization, team, project and development account used by the local sign-in flow.
docsGetStarted.exploreBody: The default UI is at {ui}, the GraphQL API at {api}, and the Temporal UI at {temporal}. Check your Compose configuration if you override host ports. Use the command wrapper to inspect running containers and logs.
docsGetStarted.checksBody: Backend tests run against real PostgreSQL and Temporal through the local stack. Ruff checks backend formatting and lint; the frontend has TypeScript, ESLint and React tests. When changing the GraphQL contract, regenerate its schema and frontend types together.
